row.name: Admiralty Inlet
row.note: 'Named by Parry, 1820, after the Board of Admiralty.' The region east of it is Tununiq, 'in the shade of the big mountain'; Ikpiarjuk (Arctic Bay) lies at its head.

row.name: Alexander Island
row.note: Findlay Group; after Viscount Alexander of Tunis, Governor General 1946-52. Board decision 1 February 1962.

row.name: Amadjuak Lake
row.note: Boas 1888 gives Amaqdjuaq, the large place where children are carried in the amauti. Grant gives Aminaarjuaq as the name of the abandoned HBC post of the same name on the south coast.

row.name: Amund Ringnes Island
row.note: Named by Sverdrup for Amund Ringnes, one of the two Christiania brewers who financed the expedition. Crossed by Isachsen and Hassel in the spring of 1901.

row.name: Archer Fiord
row.note: The long fiord running west from Lady Franklin Bay on northern Ellesmere Island, named by Nares in 1875 after Lieutenant Robert Henry Archer of HMS Discovery, who explored it. Record Point within it is 'probably so named by Lieut. Archer, who explored the fiord, after a record left there by him'.

row.name: Assistance Bay
row.note: An indentation of the south coast of Cornwallis Island a few miles west of what is now Qausuittuq (Resolute). William Penny's brigs Lady Franklin and Sophia wintered here in 1850-51, close enough to Austin's squadron for the two commanders to quarrel.

row.name: Austin Channel
row.note: After Captain Horatio Thomas Austin, who commanded the four-ship Franklin search squadron of 1850-51. Board decision 31 May 1982.

row.name: Ausuittuq
row.note: On the south coast of Ellesmere Island, 55 km north-west of Craig Harbour. The name means the place that never thaws. Founded as a community by the High Arctic relocation of 1953, when families from Inukjuak and Mittimatalik were landed at Craig Harbour; the RCMP detachment moved here from Craig Harbour in 1956.

row.name: Axel Heiberg Island
row.note: Reached and named by Sverdrup's parties in the spring of 1900 for Axel Heiberg, the Norwegian consul and financier who helped pay for the expedition. At about 43,000 square kilometres it is one of the largest islands mapped in the twentieth century; it is uninhabited, and now carries the Eureka weather station on the Ellesmere shore opposite.

row.name: Baillie-Hamilton Island
row.note: In Wellington Channel. Named by William Penny in 1851 'after Capt. W. A. Baillie-Hamilton, R.N., Secretary of the Admiralty'. Penny also put the secretary's wife, daughter and two sons on the surrounding features. Board decision 10 March 1953.

row.name: Ballantyne Strait
row.note: Between Brock and Borden islands; charted from the Canadian Arctic Expedition's sledge work. Board decision 31 May 1982.

row.name: Barbeau Peak
row.note: The highest mountain in Canada east of the Rockies, in the British Empire Range. Hattersley-Smith made the first ascent in 1967 during Operation Tanquary and named it. His obituary gives its height as 2665 m; the Canadian Geographical Names Database and Natural Resources Canada give 2616 m.

row.name: Barrow Strait
row.note: The western continuation of Lancaster Sound and the crossroads of the whole search. Every squadron passed through it; Austin wintered at its northern edge, Belcher's ships were abandoned in its ice, and the Breadalbane was crushed and sunk at its eastern end off Beechey Island.

row.name: Bathurst Island
row.note: The large island west of Cornwallis Island. M'Dougall's sledge Beaufort proved in April 1851 that Bathurst and Cornwallis are joined round the head of the bay between them, and Aldrich's sledge Lady Franklin followed its west coast north to latitude 76 deg 15 min N that spring.

row.name: Beechey Island
row.note: Franklin's first winter quarters, 1845-46, at the mouth of Wellington Channel. Found by the searchers in August 1850: three graves, tent circles, a forge, sledge tracks and some 700 empty meat tins, but no written record of where the ships meant to go.

row.name: Belcher Channel
row.note: Between Devon and Cornwall islands; after Sir Edward Belcher, who commanded the 1852-54 squadron and named much of the surrounding coast. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Bellot Strait
row.note: The narrow channel, about eighteen miles long, separating Somerset Island from the Boothia Peninsula. Kennedy and Bellot crossed it on 6-7 April 1852 and Kennedy named it for his young French second (Short Narrative p. 132). Kennedy did not understand what he had found: he called the southern shore Levesque Island, so he did not realise he had stood on the tip of the continent, and he went home wrongly convinced that North Somerset and Prince of Wales Land were joined. That the strait's south shore carries Murchison Promontory, the northernmost point of mainland North America, was established afterwards. McClintock later took the Fox to its eastern mouth.

row.name: Boothia Peninsula
row.note: Named Boothia Felix by John Ross for his backer Felix Booth. The Netsilingmiut - the people of the seal - live here; the modern communities are Taloyoak (Spence Bay) and Kugaaruk (Pelly Bay). Ross's four winters were spent on its east coast and James Clark Ross's sledge journeys crossed its isthmus to the western sea. Already entered under another topic.

row.name: Borden Island
row.note: Island in the Queen Elizabeth Islands found by Stefansson in June 1915 and named for Prime Minister Robert Borden. What Stefansson mapped as one Borden Island proved in 1947, from Royal Canadian Air Force photography, to be two: Borden and Mackenzie King Islands, divided by Wilkins Strait.

row.name: Brock Island
row.note: Island west of Borden Island in the Queen Elizabeth Islands, found by Stefansson, Storkerson and Andreasen in June 1915 travelling on the ice north of Prince Patrick Island; named for Reginald Brock, deputy minister of Mines. Cape Murray, its northwest point, became the Northern Party's landing place and meat depot for the journeys of 1916 and 1917.

row.name: Browne Island
row.note: Barrow Strait. Named by Parry in 1820 'out of respect to my much esteemed friend, Mr. Henry Browne, of Portland-Place', London. Board decision 30 June 1910.

row.name: CFS Alert
row.note: Canadian Forces Station Alert, the northernmost permanently inhabited place in the world, established as a weather station in 1950 and as a signals intelligence station in 1958. It takes its name from HMS Alert, which wintered a few kilometres away at Floeberg Beach in 1875-76, and it sits beside the Alert Global Atmosphere Watch observatory.

row.name: Cameron Island
row.note: In the Findlay Group. Dunbar and Greenaway say it is 'called after the late Chief Cartographer of Canada'. Board decision 6 June 1952. The Bent Horn field on this island was the only oil ever produced in the Canadian Arctic islands, 1985-96.

row.name: Cape Dyer
row.note: The eastern end of the DEW Line on Baffin Island: DYE-Main, its airstrip and its tropospheric scatter link across Davis Strait to Greenland. Now a North Warning System site.

row.name: Cape Mercy
row.note: At the southern entrance to Cumberland Sound on Qikiqtaaluk (Baffin Island). The abandoned Resolute, drifting alone for sixteen months, was sighted near here by the American whaler George Henry on 10 September 1855, about 1,200 miles from where her crew had left her.

row.name: Cape Walsingham
row.note: Named by Davis in 1585 after Sir Francis Walsingham (1530-90), Principal Secretary of State to Elizabeth I and a patron of the voyage.

row.name: Cape Wolstenholme
row.note: The north-west tip of Nunavik, named by Hudson in 1610 for Sir John Wolstenholme, at the corner where Hudson Strait turns into Hudson Bay. The Inuit community of Ivujivik lies just to the south.

row.name: Coats Island
row.note: 'After Captain W. Coats of the Hudson's Bay Company's service, who made many voyages to Hudson bay between 1727 and 1751.'

row.name: Cobourg Island
row.note: Island in the mouth of Jones Sound, between Ellesmere and Devon. The Craig Harbour detachment patrolled it repeatedly in 1925-26 for walrus and for the seabird colony at Cambridge Point; Stallworthy rounded it on the way to Craig Harbour in April 1931. Position from published charts, not the Canadian Geographical Names Database.

row.name: Cornwallis Island
row.note: The island on which Qausuittuq stands. Its north-east corner carried the joint Arctic weather station and airfield that made a settlement here useful to the government.

row.name: Countess of Warwick's Sound
row.note: The sound near the head of Frobisher Bay where the fleets of 1577 and 1578 anchored, named by Frobisher for Anne Dudley, Countess of Warwick, wife of his patron. Kodlunarn, Niountelik, Oopungnewing and the mainland point of Tikkoon all lie within it. Hall mapped it in 1861-62 and put an inset of it on his chart.

row.name: Craig Harbour
row.note: A small harbour on the north shore of Jones Sound, south-east Ellesmere Island, 55 km from what is now Ausuittuq (Grise Fiord). Named for Dr John D. Craig, commander of the 1922 Eastern Arctic expedition. The RCMP established a detachment here in August 1922: the northernmost police post in the world at the time and the anchor of Canada's claim to the Arctic islands. Closed in the 1930s, reopened 1951, and the landing place for the first families of the High Arctic relocation in 1953.

row.name: Crozier Channel
row.note: Between Prince Patrick and Eglinton islands; after Francis Crozier, who commanded HMS Terror and then the whole Franklin expedition after Franklin's death. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Cumberland Sound
row.note: Davis pushed sixty leagues up it in August 1585 and thought it the passage: deep water, an ocean-coloured sea, whales coming from the west and a six or seven fathom tide. It is a blind sound. Pangnirtung stands on it today.

row.name: Danish Strait
row.note: Between King Christian and Ellef Ringnes islands; named by Sverdrup in 1901 because some of his officers were Danes. Board decision 9 June 1982.

row.name: Dealy Island
row.note: A small island off the south coast of Melville Island, in Bridport Inlet. Kellett's depot from HMS Resolute, built in 1853, still stands here in ruins; the St. Roch examined it on 27 August 1944 and Joe Panipakuttuk described it in his memoir. Coordinates corrected on 2026-09-08 from 74.9/-110.85 to the Canadian Geographical Names Database value, which is consistent with Larsen's statement that Winter Harbour lies about 30 miles further west.

row.name: Devon Island
row.note: The large uninhabited island between Lancaster Sound and Jones Sound. Cook, Ahwelah and Etukishook wintered on its north coast at Cape Sparbo in 1908-09.

row.name: Digges Islands
row.note: Two islands off Cape Wolstenholme at the north-west corner of Nunavik, where Hudson Strait opens into Hudson Bay, named by Hudson in August 1610 for Sir Dudley Digges. On 28 July 1611 the returning mutineers were attacked here after trying to trade for meat and fowl; Henry Greene was killed outright and three more men died of their wounds. The islands are a major seabird colony, which is why the ship stopped.

row.name: Discovery Harbour
row.note: The harbour in Lady Franklin Bay on the Ellesmere Island shore where HMS Discovery wintered in 1875-76 under Henry Stephenson. Six years later Greely built Fort Conger on its northern shore.

row.name: Dundas Harbour
row.note: RCMP detachment on the south coast of Devon Island, opened 1924. The St. Roch called on 18-19 August 1944 to inspect the closed buildings.

row.name: Dundas Island
row.note: In Wellington Channel; named by Penny in 1851 'after Deans Dundas, one of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty'. Not the Dundas Island off British Columbia nor Dundas Harbour on Devon Island. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Eclipse Sound
row.note: 'After the whaling vessel Eclipse.' The water between Baffin Island and Bylot Island off Mittimatalik. Captain William Adams of the Arctic surveyed it in 1872.

row.name: Ellef Ringnes Island
row.note: Named for Ellef Ringnes, the second of the brewer brothers. Isachsen and Hassel reached it in 1901; the Isachsen weather station operated on its west coast from 1948 to 1978.

row.name: Ellesmere Island
row.note: Canada's northernmost island. Inuit had not lived on it permanently for centuries when the relocatees were landed on its south coast in 1953; the RCMP posts at Craig Harbour and Bache Peninsula had been there since 1922 to assert Canadian sovereignty.

row.name: Etah
row.note: The northernmost Inughuit settlement, on Foulke Fiord in the Smith Sound district of northwest Greenland. Its people fed, guided and rescued every American expedition on this coast: Kane's in 1854-55, Hayes's in 1860-61, and the Polaris survivors in 1872-73. It was abandoned as a permanent settlement in the twentieth century; the people of the district now live mainly at Siorapaluk and Qaanaaq.

row.name: Exeter Sound
row.note: On the Qikiqtaaluk (Baffin Island) coast, named by Davis on 6 August 1585 for the Exeter merchants who paid for the voyage, along with Mount Raleigh, Totnes Road, Dyer's Cape and Cape Walsingham on the same day.

row.name: Exmouth Island
row.note: In Queens Channel. Named by Belcher in August 1852 on the anniversary of Lord Exmouth's bombardment of Algiers. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Felix Harbour
row.note: The Victory's first wintering berth, on the east coast of the Boothia Peninsula near Lord Mayor Bay, where she was stopped on 1 October 1829 and lay for eleven and a half months. Named for Felix Booth. It was here that the crew met the Netsilingmiut on 9 January 1830, where Chimham Thomas made Tulluahiu's wooden leg, and where Ikmallik and Apelagliu drew the chart of Boothia. Already entered under [[topic:inuit-oral-history]].

row.name: Fitzwilliam Strait
row.note: Between Melville and Eglinton islands. Board decision 3 March 1949.

row.name: Fosheim Peninsula
row.note: The large peninsula of western Ellesmere between Eureka Sound and Greely Fiord, named after Ivar Fosheim of the Sverdrup expedition. A polar oasis with the richest muskox range in the High Arctic, and the ground the Eureka weather station works on. Board decision 9 June 1982.

row.name: Foulke Fiord
row.note: The fiord at whose mouth Etah stands, named by Isaac Hayes in 1860-61 for William Parker Foulke of Philadelphia. Four miles long, with Alida Lake at its head and Brother John's Glacier coming down into the lake. Borup Lodge stood on its shore; MacMillan gives the latitude as 78 degrees 20 minutes north.

row.name: Fury and Hecla Strait
row.historic: Strait of the Fury and Hecla
row.note: The narrow strait between Melville Peninsula and Baffin Island joining Foxe Basin to the Gulf of Boothia. Iligliuk drew it at Winter Island in 1822 before any European had seen it; Parry reached it in 1822 and named it for his ships, but never found it free of ice.

row.name: Garrett Island
row.note: Barrow Strait. Named by Parry in 1819 'out of respect to my much-esteemed friend Captain Henry Garrett' of the Royal Navy. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Griffith Island
row.note: A small island in Barrow Strait south-west of Cornwallis Island. Austin's four ships - Resolute, Assistance, Pioneer and Intrepid - froze in off its eastern shore for the winter of 1850-51, and the spring sledge campaign that mapped much of the western archipelago started from here.

row.name: Hazen Camp
row.note: The Operation Hazen base camp, on a small sandy point on the northwest shore of Lake Hazen at 81 deg 49 min N, 71 deg 18 min W (Savile 1964, p. 237). Built in 1957 for the International Geophysical Year, occupied through the winter of 1957-58 and in field seasons to 1974; later used by Parks Canada. The Canadian Geographical Names Database gives 81.8167 N, 71.3333 W for Hazen Camp.

row.name: Herbert Island
row.note: Island in Whale Sound; its settlement was inhabited into the 1980s. Not to be confused with Qeqertarsuaq (Godhavn) in Disko Bay.

row.name: Hudson Strait
row.note: The 450-mile strait between Qikiqtaaluk (Baffin Island) and Nunavik through which every voyage in this topic after Davis passed. Davis met its tide races in 1587 without entering; Hudson took the Discovery through it in 1610. Its tides are among the largest in the Arctic, which is what misled Davis and what let Baffin argue in 1615 that no passage led west out of it.

row.name: Iglulik
row.note: An island and community in northern Foxe Basin where the Fury and Hecla passed the winter of 1822-23. Parry's and Lyon's account of the Iglulingmiut here is among the earliest detailed European records of Inuit life in the eastern Arctic, and is still read in the community.

row.name: Ikpiarjuk
row.note: On the north-west coast of Qikiqtaaluk. One of the 1955 relocatee families spent a winter here in transit and did not reach Ausuittuq until 1957. Ikpiarjuk families were later moved to Qausuittuq.

row.name: Ile Vanier
row.note: In the Findlay Group; named after Georges Vanier, Governor General 1959-67, and approved by the Board on 1 February 1962, the same day as Alexander Island and Massey Island. It keeps its French form on the chart.

row.name: Ilulissat
row.note: Kalaallisut 'icebergs' (iluliaq, singular), for the ice discharged by Sermeq Kujalleq. Danish colony Jakobshavn from 1741; the Greenlandic name has been the only authorised form since 1996.

row.name: Iqaluit
row.note: The largest settlement in Qikiqtaaluk, grown around the American airbase of 1942 and the DEW Line construction of the 1950s. The QTC held its final hearings here and released its report here in 2013.

row.name: Johan Peninsula
row.note: Eastern Ellesmere, between Flagler Bay and Talbot Inlet; named by Sverdrup in 1899. Board decision 30 June 1910.

row.name: Jones Sound
row.note: The sound between Ellesmere Island and Devon Island, named by Baffin in July 1616 for Alderman Sir Francis Jones, one of the backers. Baffin saw the mouth from seaward and did not enter.

row.name: Judge Daly Promontory
row.note: The Ellesmere shore of Kennedy Channel; named by Nares in 1875 after Charles Patrick Daly, the New York judge who was president of the American Geographical Society. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Kane Basin
row.note: The wide basin between Smith Sound and Kennedy Channel. The relief steamer Proteus was crushed and sunk in its ice on 23 July 1883, and Greely's party drifted across it on the floes in September 1883. Approximate mid-basin position.

row.name: Kangiqtugaapik
row.note: On Patricia Bay off Davis Strait, eastern Qikiqtaaluk. Families from the surrounding ilagiit nunagivaktangit were drawn into the settlement in the 1960s.

row.name: Kekerten
row.note: A whaling station in Cumberland Sound from the 1850s, run for Scottish owners and latterly by Robert Kinnes and Company under Captain James Mutch. It became a trading post about 1915 and was bought by the Hudson's Bay Company in 1923 and closed about 1925. Now Kekerten Territorial Park.

row.name: Kellett Strait
row.note: Between Melville and Eglinton islands; after Henry Kellett, whose Resolute wintered at Dealy Island in 1852-53 and whose sledge parties found and named most of the western islands. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Kennedy Channel
row.note: The channel between Kane Basin and Hall Basin, named by Elisha Kent Kane's expedition for the London merchant John P. Kennedy. Position from the Canadian Geographical Names Database.

row.name: Killiniq
row.note: The southern cape of the mouth of Hudson Strait, named by Davis on 1 August 1587 for his friend John Chidley of Devon, who died in the Strait of Magellan.

row.name: Kimmirut
row.note: On the south coast of Qikiqtaaluk, on Hudson Strait. One of the eight Qikiqtani communities whose history the QTC wrote for the years 1950 to 1975.

row.name: King Christian Island
row.note: The smallest of the new islands, sighted and named on the Isachsen-Hassel journey of 1901 for King Christian IX of Denmark.

row.name: King William Island
row.note: Qikiqtaq. Rae's informants at Pelly Bay in 1854 described the party of about forty men seen dragging a boat south over the ice off its north shore in the spring of 1850. Hobson found the Victory Point record on its north-west coast on 6 May 1859. Both wrecks lie off its southern and western shores. The community of Uqsuqtuuq (Gjoa Haven) is on its south-east coast.

row.name: Kingittorsuaq Island
row.note: Uninhabited island about 3.7 by 2.7 km in the southern Upernavik Archipelago, Avannaata, northwest Greenland. Three cairns forming an equilateral triangle stood on its summit; a runestone from one of them, found in 1824 by the Greenlandic hunter Pelimut, is the northernmost Norse inscription known and the hard northern datum for the Norse in the Arctic. Coordinates from the National Museum of Denmark's record, 72.96556 N, 56.23769 W; Nansen 1911 gives 72 deg 55 min N.

row.name: Kinngait
row.note: On Dorset Island off south-west Qikiqtaaluk. The printmaking co-operative founded here in 1959 became the model the government held up for Inuit economic development.

row.name: Kodlunarn Island
row.historic: Kodlunarn Island, Countess of Warwick Sound
row.note: A small island in Countess of Warwick Sound at the head of Frobisher Bay. Martin Frobisher mined here in 1577 and 1578; his men left coal, brick, tile, a trench cut for a ship and the remains of a stone house. Hall was led to it in 1861 by Inuit who had kept the story of the kodlunas, the white men, for five generations. The name means 'white men's island'.

row.name: Kugaaruk
row.note: Pelly Bay of the charts, Okbillegeok to Schwatka's informants. It was Inuit met near here in April 1854 who first told John Rae, through William Ouligbuck, that about forty white men had died to the westward beyond a large river.

row.name: Kullorsuaq
row.note: Kalaallisut 'the large thumb', for the rock beside the settlement - the northernmost village of the Upernavik district, at the south edge of Melville Bay.

row.name: Lake Hazen
row.note: The great lake behind the Garfield Range in Grant Land, the Grant Land party's advanced base in May 1935. Moore found the ice four to five feet thick and the Arctic char smaller than Peary's account had led him to expect; five days' fishing gave too little to feed the dogs, and the shortage forced him to cut the final dash to two men and one sledge. Stallworthy and Inuatuk stayed here fishing while Moore and Nukapinguaq went north. Later the site of Operation Hazen: see [[topic:operation-hazen-1957]].

row.name: Lancaster Sound
row.note: The eastern gate of the north-west passage. Ross entered it on 30 August 1818, reported the Croker Mountains across it on the 31st and turned back; Parry sailed straight through in August 1819. Now the Tallurutiup Imanga National Marine Conservation Area.

row.name: Little Cornwallis Island
row.note: Named by extension from Cornwallis Island; the strait between the two was only found in 1947, by a USAF photographic crew. Board decision 5 September 1957. The Polaris lead-zinc mine worked here from 1982 to 2002.

row.name: Loks Land
row.note: Island at the north side of the entrance to Frobisher Bay, 'after Michael Lok, who wrote an account of Frobisher's first voyage and was one of the venturers' (White 1910). Lok was the Cathay Company's treasurer and was ruined by the worthless ore.

row.name: Lougheed Island
row.note: Island south of the Ringnes islands where Stefansson, Noice and Karsten Andersen camped from 9 August to 3 September 1916 waiting for the freeze-up, taking thirty hours of tidal observations; named for Senator James Lougheed. Their summer camp record was left at about 77 degrees 09 minutes north.

row.name: Lowther Island
row.note: Barrow Strait. Named by Parry in 1819 after Viscount Lowther, a lord of the Treasury. Bernier landed here in 1907 and named Gourdeau Point after the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Luke Sound
row.note: 'Named by Frobisher, 1578, by reason of one Luke Ward that went with him on land' (White 1910) - one of the Frobisher names given for a member of the ship's company rather than a backer.

row.name: Mackenzie King Island
row.note: Island in the Queen Elizabeth Islands. Stefansson's parties walked its coasts in 1915 and 1916 believing it the southern part of Borden Island; it was shown to be a separate island in 1947 and named for Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King.

row.name: Maclean Strait
row.note: Between Lougheed Island and the Findlay Group. Board decision 5 April 1921.

row.name: Mansel Island
row.note: A low, flat island about twenty leagues long in northern Hudson Bay, west of the Digges Islands. Coats put its south-west point in latitude 61 degrees 40 minutes north; ships bound for Churchill passed to the west of it.

row.name: Massey Island
row.note: Findlay Group; after Vincent Massey, Governor General 1952-59. Board decision 1 February 1962. Distinct from Massey Sound, which is between Amund Ringnes and Axel Heiberg islands.

row.name: Meighen Island
row.note: Uninhabited ice-capped island north of the Ringnes islands, about 950 square kilometres. First sighted by Karsten Andersen on 12 June 1916 and landed on by Harold Noice at about 3 a.m. on 15 June 1916, from a party of three led by Stefansson travelling north from Cape Isachsen. The last substantial island added to the map of Arctic Canada from the sea ice.

row.name: Melville Bay
row.note: The great bight in the north-east corner of Baffin Bay, between Kap York and Upernavik: no harbours, calving glaciers, and a pack that closes on ships against the land floe. Whalers crossed it every spring to reach the North Water and the west-side grounds, and it cost them more ships than any other place in the fishery — fourteen in 1819, about twenty in 1830, and more in 1835-37.

row.name: Melville Island
row.historic: Melville Island; one of Parry's North Georgian Islands, 1819
row.note: The island at the west end of Parry Channel; Bernier's Arctic wintered at Winter Harbour on its south coast in 1908-09, where Parry's Hecla and Griper had wintered in 1819-20. See [[topic:ross-parry]].

row.name: Melville Peninsula
row.note: Named by Parry after Robert Saunders Dundas, 2nd Viscount Melville, First Lord of the Admiralty 1812-27 and 1828-30 - the same man as Melville Island, Cape Dundas and Dundas Peninsula. Winter Island, where Parry wintered in 1821-22 and where Iligliuk drew him her chart, lies off its east coast.

row.name: Mercy Bay
row.note: Bay on the north coast of Banks Island where McClure's Investigator was abandoned in 1853; Stefansson's party visited the site in 1915 and 1916 and found the Admiralty chart of the coast badly wrong.

row.name: Meta Incognita Peninsula
row.note: The peninsula between Frobisher Bay and Hudson Strait. Named in Latin by Elizabeth I in 1577 for the whole of Frobisher's discovery: 'the unknown limit'. The oldest surviving European name in the Canadian Arctic.

row.name: Milne Inlet
row.note: 'Named by Bernier, 1906, after Capt. W. F. Milne of the whaling steamer Eclipse.' It is now the shipping route for the Mary River iron mine and the subject of the Pond Inlet community's shipping-risk work.

row.name: Mittimatalik
row.note: The Inuit community at the north end of Qikiqtaaluk (Baffin Island). Bernier's crews wintered nearby at Albert Harbour and traded with families here; the Scottish whaling station and later the trading posts grew from the same anchorage.

row.name: Mould Bay
row.historic: Mould Bay (Mecham, 1853, at the request of Nares)
row.note: On the east side of Prince Patrick Island. Named by Lieutenant Mecham in 1853, at the request of Mr G. S. Nares, during the sledge surveys from Dealy Island; the blue book prints the naming in Mecham's list of names given to new discoveries. A century later it was one of the Joint Arctic Weather Stations - see [[topic:science-stations]] - and it is still one of the very few places on Prince Patrick Island anybody has lived.

row.name: Mount Aqiatushuk
row.note: The mountain near Ausuittuq at the base of which Patrick Aqiattusuk, one of the Inukjuak people moved to Ellesmere Island in 1953, is buried. The Inuit Heritage Trust records the name as Aqiattusuk; the official form is Mount Aqiatushuk.

row.name: Mount Raleigh
row.note: Named by Davis in 1585 after Sir Walter Raleigh, one of the promoters of his voyages, on the coast of Cumberland Peninsula.

row.name: Naujaat
row.note: Naujaat, 'the nesting place of seagulls', at the head of Repulse Bay on the Arctic Circle. Parry landed here on 22 August 1821 after forcing the Frozen Strait and proved the land continuous, closing one of the last hopes of a passage out of the top of Hudson Bay. It was the goal Lyon failed to reach in the Griper in 1824. Parry's own observed position for his landing was 66 deg 30 min 58 sec N, 86 deg 30 min 20 sec W; the coordinates here are those of the modern community.

row.name: Navy Board Inlet
row.note: Named by Parry in 1820 after the Navy Board, the civil department that built and supplied the ships. Adams Island at its entrance is Tuujjuk; Canada Point on its west side is Titiralik, 'where there is writing', for the inscription Bernier's men cut there.

row.name: Nerky
row.note: An Inughuit settlement about forty-five miles south of Etah, and one of the expedition's regular stopping places on the road to North Star Bay.

row.name: Nettilling Lake
row.note: The largest lake on Baffin Island. Boas 1888 glosses Nettilling as 'with seals' - nattiq, the ringed seal, which lives in it. White 1910 wrongly calls it 'Indian name, meaning flat floor'. The official name is registered as Inuktitut.

row.name: Nottingham Island
row.note: A low island of about 200 square miles at the western end of Hudson Strait, between Digges Islands and Southampton Island, named by Hudson in 1610. The western base of the Hudson Strait Expedition, 1927-28, and later a Canadian weather and radio station.

row.name: Nuuk
row.note: Kalaallisut 'point; foreland'. The Danish colony founded on it by Hans Egede in 1728 was Godthaab, 'good hope'; Davis had called the fiord Gilbert Sound in 1585. Only the Greenlandic form has been authorised since 1 January 1996.

row.name: Nuup Kangerlua
row.note: The fjord system at Nuuk in west Greenland, which Davis named Gilbert Sound in 1585 for Sir Humphrey Gilbert. All three voyages anchored here, and it is where the music and dancing, the wrestling, the trading and both kidnappings happened.

row.name: Panniqtuuq
row.note: On Cumberland Sound. In 1962 a distemper epidemic and the shooting of dogs by police and others left many Panniqtuuq families without a team; the community was also a hub of the tuberculosis patrols and held a nursing station.

row.name: Peary Channel
row.note: Between Ellef Ringnes and Meighen islands; after Robert E. Peary. Board decision 12 December 1939.

row.name: Penny Strait
row.note: Between Bathurst and Devon islands; after the whaling captain William Penny, who searched Wellington Channel in 1850-51 and named most of its shores. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Pituffik
row.note: The American air base in northwest Greenland, built from 1946, from which every one of the Canadian weather stations was flown in and supplied. The Inughuit of Uummannaq were moved from the site in 1953 to make room for it.

row.name: Ponds Inlet
row.note: The water, as distinct from the hamlet. 'Named by John Ross, 1818, after John Ponds (1767-1836), Astronomer-Royal' - White's spelling; the man was John Pond. Ponds Inlet is recorded by the Names Database as a previously official form of the inlet.

row.name: Prince Patrick Island
row.note: The westernmost of the Queen Elizabeth Islands, charted by Mecham and McClintock on foot from the Resolute's winter quarters at Dealy Island in 1853. Nobody was looking for it; it was found because men were dragging sledges across the ice looking for Franklin.

row.name: Qaanaaq
row.note: The main settlement of Avanersuaq, built in 1953 about 130 km north of Uummannaq to house the people moved out of the way of the American airbase. Roughly 600 people live here.

row.name: Qatiktalik
row.note: Fullerton Harbour, on Roes Welcome Sound, was the principal American wintering harbour in northwestern Hudson Bay after about 1900; George Comer wintered the Era here repeatedly. The North-West Mounted Police put their first Hudson Bay post beside the whalers here in 1903.

row.name: Qausuittuq
row.note: On Cornwallis Island beside the joint Canadian-American weather station and airfield opened in 1947. Half the 1953 relocatees were put ashore here, the other half at Craig Harbour. The name means 'the place with no dawn'.

row.name: Qeqertarsuaq
row.note: On Disko Island, west Greenland. The Gjoa took on dogs, sledges and Greenlandic clothing here in late July 1903, with help from the Danish inspector Daugaard-Jensen, and sailed on 31 July.

row.name: Qikiqtarjuaq
row.note: 'The big island'. John Ross named Broughton Island in 1818 'after a friend', identified by White 1910 as Commodore William Robert Broughton. The hamlet took back the Inuktitut name in 1998; Broughton Island is recorded as previously official.

row.name: Qimusseriarsuaq
row.note: The great bay of glaciers between Upernavik and Cape York; the barrier that separated the Inughuit from the Danish colonies to the south. The Inughuit name means 'the great dog-driving place'.

row.name: Queen Elizabeth Islands
row.note: The group north of Parry Channel, about 419,000 sq km, renamed in 1953 after Elizabeth II on her coronation as Queen of Canada. 'Parry Islands' survives as an official name for the southern part of the group. CGNDB decision 23 November 1983.

row.name: Quttinirpaaq National Park
row.note: Quttinirpaaq means roughly 'the top of the world'. Set aside as Ellesmere Island National Park Reserve in 1988 over the country Operation Hazen and Operation Tanquary worked in, and made a national park in 2000; the park's two operating bases, Tanquary Fiord and Lake Hazen, are the two Defence Research Board camps.

row.name: Raanes Peninsula
row.note: Western Ellesmere; after Oluf Raanes, mate of the Fram. Board decision 9 July 1982.

row.name: Repulse Bay
row.note: Naujaat, at the head of Roes Welcome Sound. Rae wintered here in 1846-47 and again in 1853-54, and it was here in the summer of 1854 that he bought the Franklin relics and took down the testimony he sent to the Admiralty on 29 July. Now a community of about a thousand people on the Arctic Circle.

row.name: Robeson Channel
row.note: The northernmost reach of Nares Strait, between Ellesmere Island and Greenland, opening on the Lincoln Sea. Nares forced both his ships through it in August 1875; its ice defeated every later attempt to reach Fort Conger from the south.

row.name: Salisbury Island
row.note: An island at the western end of Hudson Strait between Nottingham Island and the Baffin shore, named by Hudson in 1610.

row.name: Salliq
row.note: Southampton Island, the home of the Sadlermiut. The modern community of Salliq (Coral Harbour) is on its south coast; the island was resettled from Aivilik and from Nunavik after the Sadlermiut died in the winter of 1902-03.

row.name: Sanderson's Hope
row.note: The headland near Upernavik that Davis reached on 30 June 1587 in 72 deg 12 min, his farthest north and the northernmost point any European had then made on this coast. He left it with the sea open west and north, and ran into the middle pack.

row.name: Sanirajak
row.note: 'The shoreline', a place along the coast. The English name was for Charles Francis Hall. The hamlet's official name became Sanirajak in 2020; Hall Beach is recorded as previously official.

row.name: Savissivik
row.note: Settlement on the south side of Melville Bay near Cape York. The name means 'the place where one gets knife-metal' - the Inughuit quarried iron here from the Cape York meteorites for centuries.

row.name: Schei Peninsula
row.note: The peninsula on the north-east side of Axel Heiberg Island between Bay Fiord and Nansen Sound. Krüger collected specimen 160 here on 8 April 1930 and others, undated, from its west side; it is one of the points the rock labels put beyond doubt. Position approximate, for the middle of the peninsula.

row.name: Sherard Osborn Island
row.note: In Penny Strait; after Sherard Osborn of the Austin and Belcher expeditions, whose Stray Leaves from an Arctic Journal is one of the few search narratives that records how names were given. Board decision 3 April 1959.

row.name: Sheriff's Harbour
row.note: The second wintering berth, about four miles north of Felix Harbour, cut into through October 1830 at a rate of a few dozen feet a day and abandoned as a project on 31 October with two hundred yards still to go. Named for Felix Booth as Sheriff of London; Ross records that those fond of puns thought the name apt. Position inferred from the four miles of northing the ship made, not observed.

row.name: Simmons Peninsula
row.note: South-western Ellesmere; after Herman Georg Simmons, the Swedish botanist of the Sverdrup expedition. Not to be confused with Simmons Bay and Simmons Point, which are named after two petty officers of the Nares expedition. Board decision 30 June 1910.

row.name: Siorapaluk
row.note: On the north shore of Robertson Fjord; the northernmost settlement in the world with a permanent civilian population.

row.name: Sisimiut
row.note: Kalaallisut, glossed by the Greenland Pilot as 'the place with fox dens'. Danish colony Holsteinsborg from 1756.

row.name: Smith Sound
row.note: The channel at the head of Baffin Bay between Ellesmere Island and north-west Greenland, named by Baffin in July 1616 at his farthest north. It is the entrance to the route later used by Kane, Hayes, Hall, Nares and Peary, and the crossing place of the Inughuit.

row.name: Somerset Island
row.note: 'Named by Parry, 1820, North Somerset, after his native county in England.' One of the very few Arctic names Parry took from his own life rather than from the Admiralty list.

row.name: Somerville Island
row.note: Barrow Strait. Named by Parry in 1820 'after his friend, Dr. Somerville'. Board decision 30 June 1910.

row.name: Svendsen Peninsula
row.note: Western Ellesmere; after Johan Svendsen, surgeon of the Fram, who shot himself at Fram Havn in 1899. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Sverdrup Islands
row.note: Axel Heiberg, Amund Ringnes, Ellef Ringnes, King Christian and their neighbours, discovered and named by the second Fram expedition 1898-1902. Board decision 30 June 1910. Norway did not renounce its claim to them until 1930, when Canada paid Sverdrup 67,000 dollars for his charts and papers; the Sverdrup Basin beneath them still carries his name in the geological literature.

row.name: Table Island
row.note: Descriptive; north of Bathurst Island. Board decision 31 December 1910.

row.name: Tallurutiup Imanga
row.note: The National Marine Conservation Area agreed in 2019 over Lancaster Sound and its approaches, about 108,000 square kilometres, the largest protected area in Canada. It is a polynya-rich water with narwhal, beluga, bowhead, walrus and the seabird colonies of Prince Leopold Island, and it lies across the eastern gate of the North-West Passage.

row.name: Taloyoak
row.note: Community on the Boothia Peninsula. Louie Kamookak was born in 1959 at a seal-hunting camp near here, and much of the Nattilik oral tradition about the Franklin retreat was held by families of this coast.

row.name: Tanquary Fiord
row.note: A fiord running nearly thirty miles northwest into Grant Land, explored by Ekblaw in May 1915 and named by him for Maurice Tanquary. He found the ruins of Inuit dwellings, caches and fox traps on its shores. It is now the site of the Tanquary Fiord station in Quttinirpaaq National Park.

row.name: Terror Bay
row.note: On the south-west coast of King William Island. The wreck of HMS Terror was found in the middle of the bay on 3 September 2016 in about 24 m of water. The bay was named in 1910, long before the ship was found in it. A large camp site with human remains was recorded on its shore by the search parties.

row.name: The North Water
row.note: Markham's definition, 1873: 'the open water into which the vessels emerge after passing through the ice in Melville Bay.' The polynya at the head of Baffin Bay, open all winter; reaching it in May or June was the object of the Melville Bay passage, and from it ships crossed to the West Water on the Canadian side.

row.name: Truro Island
row.note: Barrow Strait, off the south-west corner of Devon Island; Brooman Point on it holds one of the best-known Late Dorset and early Thule sites in the archipelago. Board decision 30 June 1910.

row.name: Upernavik
row.note: The northernmost Danish trading settlement in Greenland in the nineteenth century, and the goal of every retreat down Baffin Bay. Kane's boat party reached it on 6 August 1855, eighty-three days after leaving the Advance. Hall, Hayes and the Polaris all called here on the way north.

row.name: Uqsuqtuuq
row.note: The community on the south-east coast of King William Island nearest the wrecks and the death march. Louie Kamookak lived here and gathered the oral history that guided the 2014 search; Sammy Kogvik of Gjoa Haven redirected the 2016 search into Terror Bay.

row.name: Uumanarjuaq
row.note: A small bare island of graphite-bearing rock on the south side of Cumberland Sound. Crawford Noble of Aberdeen bought the whaling station here in 1894 and gave the Church Missionary Society a free passage and a place to build; E. J. Peck and J. C. Parker landed on 21 August 1894 and made it the first permanent Christian mission on Qikiqtaaluk (Baffin Island). Designated the Blacklead Island Whaling Station National Historic Site in 1985.

row.name: Uummannaq
row.note: Kalaallisut 'similar to a heart', for the mountain over the settlement. Danish colony from 1758.

row.name: Uummannaq (Thule)
row.note: The settlement under the flat-topped mountain Uummannaq on North Star Bay, where Rasmussen and Freuchen built the Thule trading station in 1910. Its people were moved to Qaanaaq in 1953 and the site is now inside the airbase perimeter. Distinct from the Uummannaq in central West Greenland.

row.name: Victoria Harbour
row.note: The third and last berth of the Victory, reached at the end of August 1831 and settled into for the winter by 15 October. Ross named it Victory Harbour after his ship; it was renamed Victoria Harbour by permission of the Duchess of Kent and the Princess Victoria. The ship was abandoned here on 29 May 1832 with her colours nailed to the mast, and there she remains. Position from James Clark Ross's magnetic table; the narrative's latitude for the harbour entered on 29 August 1831 is 70 deg 18 min 11 sec and the two do not agree.

row.name: Wilmot and Crampton Bay
row.note: The wreck of HMS Erebus lies here in about 11 m of water off the Adelaide Peninsula, found on 2 September 2014. The area is closed to the public; Parks Canada gives a bounded protected zone rather than a position. The Inuit name for the district is Utjulik.

row.name: Winter Harbour
row.note: On the south coast of Melville Island. The Hecla and Griper cut a canal more than two miles long to reach it on 26 September 1819 and lay there until 1 August 1820, the first European ships to winter deliberately in the high Arctic archipelago. Parry's Rock, on which the visit is cut, stands above the beach.

row.name: Young Island
row.note: Barrow Strait. Named by Parry in 1819 after Dr Thomas Young, Secretary to the Board of Longitude - the physicist and decipherer of hieroglyphs. Board decision 30 June 1910.
